text:
Yes — a portable power station can work as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your computer, but only if it supports sufficiently fast automatic switchover. The key isn't just battery capacity or wattage; it's whether your computer stays powered when the electricity fails.

Based on the search results you provided, here’s what to look for without doing any additional web searches.

What matters most

Feature

	

What to look for




Automatic switchover

	

The station switches to battery power automatically when grid power fails.




Transfer time

	

Prefer a short, manufacturer-documented time. A brief interruption can still restart some computers.




Pure sine wave output

	

Recommended for powering sensitive computer equipment.




Pass-through operation

	

The station can safely power connected devices while charging from the wall.




Power capacity

	

Enough continuous watts for your computer, monitors, and other connected equipment.




Battery capacity

	

Enough watt-hours (Wh) to keep everything running for your desired backup duration.

Sources: Anker SOLIX's UPS guidance and EcoFlow's UPS guide.

Portable power station vs. dedicated UPS

Portable power station

Potentially hours of computer runtime.

Useful for extended outages and other appliances.

Transfer time and UPS behavior vary by model.

Often larger and heavier than a dedicated UPS.

Dedicated UPS

Designed for short interruptions and orderly computer shutdowns.

Often includes surge protection and voltage regulation.

Usually the safer choice for sensitive equipment that requires uninterrupted power.

An important distinction: a large battery does not guarantee UPS-quality protection. EcoFlow's guide warns that some power stations have switchover times of 30 ms or more, which may be too slow for some equipment. Anker's guidance similarly stresses that the connected device must tolerate the published transfer time.

Sources: EcoFlow, Anker SOLIX.

My recommendation

For a desktop PC and monitors: A UPS-capable power station can be a good option if the transfer time is compatible with your computer.

For a gaming PC or workstation: Check actual power draw, including transient spikes, and confirm the station's UPS behavior.

For a NAS or critical server: Consider a dedicated online double-conversion UPS if you require zero transfer time or continuous voltage and frequency regulation.

One question to help me recommend the right setup: Are you backing up a Windows desktop, a gaming PC, or a Mac?
